top_level_objectives: Apply VSEPR theory to predict electron-domain geometry from Lewis structures.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry when lone pairs are present.
Relate idealized and observed bond angles to electron-pair repulsion and lone-pair effects.
Compare VSEPR predictions with the 3D structures of common molecules.

scenes.scene_name: From Lewis Structure to Electron Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the central idea that a Lewis structure can be translated into regions of electron density around a central atom.
key_visuals: A simple Lewis structure centered on one atom with bonded atoms and lone pairs highlighted
A clear count of electron domains around the central atom
A 3D atom model floating beside the 2D structure
student_actions: Identify the central atom and count bonding and lone-pair domains.
Use the domain count to predict the basic electron arrangement around the atom.

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how two and three electron domains spread out to minimize repulsion in a flat or straight arrangement.
key_visuals: Two-domain and three-domain models settling into linear and trigonal planar shapes
Side-by-side comparison of electron-domain geometry versus the same arrangement with and without lone pairs
student_actions: Manipulate the electron domains to see them separate as far as possible.
Match each domain count to the correct ideal geometry.

scenes.brief_purpose: Build the tetrahedral case and then show how lone pairs compress bond angles to create common molecular shapes.
key_visuals: A water-like bent shape and an ammonia-like trigonal pyramidal shape emerging from the same tetrahedral electron-domain geometry
Bond-angle readouts contrasting ideal and actual angles
student_actions: Place four domains around the central atom and observe the tetrahedral arrangement.
Remove or relabel domains as lone pairs to see how molecular geometry changes from tetrahedral to bent or trigonal pyramidal.

scenes.brief_purpose: Extend VSEPR to five electron domains and demonstrate how different placements of lone pairs lead to seesaw and T-shaped geometries.
key_visuals: A trigonal bipyramidal framework with axial and equatorial positions clearly distinguished
Animated lone pairs preferring equatorial positions
Resulting seesaw and T-shaped molecular shapes
student_actions: Experiment with five domains and identify axial versus equatorial sites.
Predict which positions lone pairs should occupy and test the resulting geometry.

scenes.scene_name: Octahedral Family and Square Planar Shapes
scenes.brief_purpose: Show the six-domain octahedral arrangement and how two lone pairs can produce square planar or square pyramidal geometries.
key_visuals: An octahedral arrangement with opposite positions highlighted
A square planar structure associated with four bonding pairs and two lone pairs
A square pyramidal alternative for comparison
student_actions: Arrange six domains to form the octahedral electron geometry.
Move lone pairs into favorable positions and observe how the molecular shape changes.

scenes.brief_purpose: Connect VSEPR predictions to actual molecular examples and reinforce why lone pairs compress bond angles more than bonding pairs.
key_visuals: Side-by-side 3D models of water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, and XeF4
Labels naming each molecule and its predicted geometry
Angle comparisons such as 104.5° in water versus 109.5° in methane
student_actions: Classify each molecule by electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Compare predicted and observed structures, then explain differences in bond angles using lone-pair repulsion.
